content: A superacid is defined as an acid with an acidity greater than that of 100% sulfuric acid, which has a Hammett acidity function (H₀) of -12. This means that superacids possess more negative H₀ values than sulfuric acid. The strongest superacids are typically synthesized by combining two components: a strong Lewis acid and a strong Brønsted acid. The term superacid was first introduced by James Bryant Conant in 1927 to describe acids that are stronger than conventional mineral acids. George A. Olah was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1994 for his groundbreaking research on superacids and their application in the direct observation of carbocations. One of Olah's notable contributions was the development of magic acid, a superacid capable of protonating hydrocarbons, which are typically non-basic. Magic acid is prepared by mixing antimony pentafluoride (SbF₅) with fluorosulfuric acid (HSO₃F). The name magic acid originated when one of Olah's postdoctoral associates placed a candle into a sample of the acid, and the candle dissolved, demonstrating the acid's extraordinary ability to protonate hydrocarbons. The strongest known superacid system is fluoroantimonic acid, which is a combination of hydrogen fluoride (HF) and antimony pentafluoride (SbF₅). In this system, HF donates its proton (H⁺), while the fluoride ion (F⁻) is stabilized by SbF₅, forming the anion SbF₆⁻. This anion is both a weak nucleophile and a weak base, leaving the proton effectively naked, which accounts for the extreme acidity of the system. Fluoroantimonic acid is approximately 2 × 10¹⁹ times stronger than 100% sulfuric acid and can produce solutions with a pH as low as -25. Olah demonstrated that at 140°C (284°F), the superacid system FSO₃H-SbF₅ can convert methane into the tertiary-butyl carbocation. This reaction begins with the protonation of methane, showcasing the unique reactivity of superacids. Superacids have numerous practical applications. They are commonly used to create and stabilize organic cations, which serve as intermediates in various chemical reactions. These reactions are particularly important in the production of plastics, high-octane gasoline, and other industrial processes.
